title: Thai cooking ingredients in Sri Lanka: curry pastes, fish sauce and noodles
seoTitle: Thai Cooking Ingredients in Sri Lanka: Pastes, Fish Sauce, Noodles
description: What a restaurant or hotel kitchen in Sri Lanka needs to cook Thai food: curry pastes, fish sauce, soy sauce and rice noodles, how each is used, and where to buy them wholesale.
summary: To cook Thai food in Sri Lanka, a professional kitchen needs four imported building blocks: curry pastes, fish sauce, soy sauce and dried rice noodles. Olive Foods imports and distributes all four (Mae Ploy curry and tom yum pastes, Tiparos fish sauce, dark soy sauce, Mahachai pad thai noodles and Wai Wai rice vermicelli) and supplies them to hotels, restaurants and caterers island-wide. Most of the fresh ingredients, such as lemongrass, chillies, coriander, limes, tamarind and coconut milk, are easy to find locally.

sections.heading: Curry pastes: the base of every Thai curry
paragraphs: A Thai curry paste is a ground blend of chillies, aromatics such as lemongrass, galangal, garlic and shallot, dried spices and, in most traditional recipes, shrimp paste. Making it by hand takes time and a mortar, so most restaurant kitchens, in Thailand and abroad, use a ready-made paste and spend their effort on the finish.

Green curry paste is made with fresh green chillies and herbs, and tastes bright and herbal. Red curry paste is made with dried red chillies, for a deeper, rounder heat that suits beef, duck, chicken and pumpkin. Tom yum paste carries the lemongrass, galangal, lime and chilli of the hot and sour soup, and also works in stir-fries and seafood marinades.

To cook a curry, fry the paste in a little thick coconut cream until it smells fragrant and the oil starts to separate, then add the rest of the coconut milk, the meat or vegetables, and season with fish sauce and palm sugar. Commercial pastes differ in strength, so start with less than you think and taste as you go.
items: Most curry pastes contain shrimp paste: check the label when cooking for vegetarian guests or anyone with a shellfish allergy.
Once opened, keep paste sealed in the refrigerator and use a clean spoon each time.

sections.heading: Fish sauce: the salt of Thai cooking
paragraphs: Fish sauce (nam pla) is made by fermenting fish, usually anchovies, with salt for many months, then drawing off the clear amber liquid. It seasons almost every savoury Thai dish, adding salt and a deep savoury flavour that disappears into the food rather than tasting fishy.

Use it in curries, stir-fries, soups, salad dressings and dipping sauces. A simple table sauce, prik nam pla, is fish sauce with sliced chillies and a squeeze of lime. Tiparos fish sauce is made in Thailand by Tang Sang Hah Co., Ltd. Keep the bottle closed and away from heat; it darkens slowly with age.

sections.heading: Soy sauces: colour and seasoning
paragraphs: Dark soy sauce is thicker and slightly sweet, and is used more for colour than salt: it gives pad see ew and braised dishes their deep brown finish. Light soy sauce seasons without darkening the dish. Olive Foods supplies a dark soy sauce for Thai and Chinese cooking.

sections.heading: Rice noodles: pad thai and vermicelli
paragraphs: Pad thai uses flat dried rice sticks. Soak them in warm water until they bend without snapping but are still firm, drain, then stir-fry them with the sauce so they finish cooking in the pan. Soaked too long, they turn mushy in the wok. The classic sauce is tamarind, fish sauce and palm sugar, and tamarind is easy to buy in Sri Lanka.

Rice vermicelli is much thinner. It needs only a short soak in hot water before it goes into stir-fries, noodle soups, fresh spring rolls and noodle salads. Mahachai pad thai noodles and Wai Wai rice vermicelli are both made from rice flour.

sections.heading: What to buy locally
paragraphs: Lemongrass, chillies, garlic, shallots, coriander, limes, tamarind and coconut milk are all easy to source in Sri Lanka. Galangal and makrut lime leaves can be harder to find; Thai curry pastes usually already contain both, so a kitchen can manage without them fresh. Thai basil can be replaced with local sweet basil in a pinch.

faqs.a: Olive Foods imports Mae Ploy green curry, red curry and tom yum pastes and supplies them to restaurants, hotels and caterers across Sri Lanka. Send a quote request with the products and quantities you need and the team replies with trade pricing and delivery details.

faqs.q: What is the difference between green and red Thai curry paste?
faqs.a: Green curry paste is made with fresh green chillies and herbs and tastes bright and herbal. Red curry paste is made with dried red chillies and has a deeper, rounder heat. Both are cooked the same way, fried in coconut cream and simmered in coconut milk.

faqs.q: Is fish sauce the same as soy sauce?
faqs.a: No. Fish sauce is made by fermenting fish with salt; soy sauce is made by fermenting soybeans, usually with wheat. Thai cooking uses fish sauce as its main salty seasoning and soy sauce mainly for colour and for Chinese-influenced dishes.

title: Buying frozen food for a hotel kitchen: a cold-chain checklist
seoTitle: Frozen Food for Hotels in Sri Lanka: A Cold-Chain Checklist
description: How hotel and restaurant kitchens in Sri Lanka keep frozen food safe and at its best: what −18 °C means, what to ask a supplier, what to check on delivery, and how to store and thaw.
summary: Frozen food keeps its safety and quality only if it stays at −18 °C or colder at every step, from the producer's freezer to your kitchen. For a hotel or restaurant that means choosing a supplier with a real cold chain, checking every frozen delivery before it goes into the freezer, storing at −18 °C, and thawing meat in the refrigerator. Olive Foods stores and delivers its frozen range (meat, poultry, fries, potato products, vegetables, fruit and purees) at −18 °C.

sections.heading: Why −18 °C matters
paragraphs: −18 °C is the temperature used around the world for storing frozen food. At −18 °C or below, microbes cannot grow, but freezing does not kill them, and quality still declines slowly over time. Temperature swings do the most visible damage: each time frozen food partly thaws and refreezes, ice crystals grow larger and break down its structure. Meat loses juice when it cooks, vegetables turn soft, fries go limp and packs develop freezer burn. Follow the storage directions on each label, and refuse any delivery that looks as if it has thawed.

sections.heading: Before you order: questions for a supplier
items: Where is frozen stock held, and at what temperature?
How is it delivered: in refrigerated or freezer vehicles, and how long is it on the road to you?
What shelf life is left on products when they arrive?
Can the supplier keep the same products in stock all year, so menus don't have to change?
Are pack sizes suited to your freezer space and how fast you use them?
Can they provide product specifications, ingredients and allergen information, and halal certificates where you need them?

sections.heading: On delivery: what to check
items: Products are hard-frozen, at or close to −18 °C. Use a probe thermometer between packs, not inside them.
No signs of thawing and refreezing: large ice crystals or frost inside bags, fries or vegetables frozen into clumps, frozen liquid pooled in a corner, or swollen or deformed cartons.
Packs are intact and labels and best-before dates are readable.
Frozen goods go straight into the freezer. Don't leave them on the loading bay while dry goods are checked.

sections.heading: In your freezer
items: Keep freezers at −18 °C or colder and record the temperature at least twice a day.
Don't overload them: cold air must circulate around the stock.
Rotate stock so the earliest best-before date is used first.
Keep raw meat and poultry below ready-to-eat and cooked foods.
Keep doors closed and plan deliveries so stock goes in quickly.

sections.heading: Thawing and cooking
paragraphs: Thaw meat, poultry and fruit purees slowly in the refrigerator, never at room temperature, and allow enough time: a large joint can take a day or more. Fries, hash browns, wedges and most vegetables are cooked straight from frozen. Meat that has been thawed in the refrigerator can be refrozen, though it loses some quality; meat thawed any other way should be cooked before it is frozen again.

faqs.q: What temperature should frozen food be delivered at?
faqs.a: Frozen food should arrive hard-frozen, at or close to −18 °C, with no signs of thawing. Olive Foods stores and delivers its frozen range at −18 °C.

faqs.q: Can you refreeze frozen meat after it has thawed?
faqs.a: Meat thawed in the refrigerator can be refrozen, but it loses some quality. Meat thawed at room temperature or in water should be cooked before freezing again.

faqs.q: Which frozen foods should be cooked from frozen?
faqs.a: Frozen fries, hash browns, potato wedges and most frozen vegetables are cooked straight from frozen. Thawing them first makes them soak up oil or turn soft.

title: Frozen fruit purees for cocktails, smoothies and pastry
seoTitle: Frozen Fruit Purees in Sri Lanka: For Bars, Cafés and Pastry
description: How bars, cafés and pastry kitchens in Sri Lanka use frozen fruit purees: how they help keep recipes consistent, which flavour suits what, and how to thaw and store them.
summary: Frozen fruit puree is fruit that has been washed, pulped, strained and frozen, so a kitchen can make the same recipe all year, whatever the fruit season. Bars use it for cocktails and mocktails, cafés for smoothies and shakes, and pastry kitchens for mousses, sorbets, glazes and fillings. Olive Foods imports and distributes DIRA purees from Dirafrost (mango, passion fruit, strawberry, raspberry, lemon and coconut) and delivers them frozen at −18 °C.

sections.heading: Why kitchens and bars use purees
items: The same flavour, sweetness and colour every time, so a drink or dessert tastes the same in March and in October.
Fruits that are out of season, or not widely grown in Sri Lanka, such as raspberries and strawberries, are available all year.
No peeling, pitting, blending or straining seeds, and no wasted fruit.
Easy to measure, so recipes and drink specs stay consistent between staff.

sections.heading: Bars: cocktails and mocktails
paragraphs: Passion fruit, strawberry and mango are the bar workhorses: daiquiris, margaritas, martinis, mojitos, coolers and alcohol-free spritzers. A typical starting point is 20–30 ml of puree per drink, adjusted with sugar syrup and citrus to taste. Coconut puree makes a fresher piña colada than canned cream of coconut.

sections.heading: Cafés: smoothies and shakes
paragraphs: Blend puree with yoghurt or milk and ice for smoothies and shakes, or combine it with whole frozen berries for texture. Mango and passion fruit together make a popular tropical smoothie; strawberry and raspberry go into milkshakes and frappés.

sections.heading: Pastry: mousses, glazes, sorbets and fillings
paragraphs: Pastry chefs use purees for fruit mousses (puree folded with whipped cream and set with gelatine), sorbets (puree with sugar syrup), mirror glazes, coulis, curds, cake soaks and the centres of macarons and chocolates. Because the fruit content is consistent, a recipe that works once works every time.

head: Puree
Good for
rows: Coulis, sorbet, macaron and chocolate fillings, vinaigrettes

sections.heading: Thawing, storing and using
items: Keep purees frozen at −18 °C until needed.
Thaw overnight in the refrigerator, not at room temperature.
Once thawed, keep the puree chilled and use it within the time on the pack; don't refreeze it.
Stir or shake before use, as solids can settle.

faqs.q: Where can I buy frozen fruit puree in Sri Lanka?
faqs.a: Olive Foods imports and distributes DIRA frozen fruit purees in mango, passion fruit, strawberry, raspberry, lemon and coconut, and delivers them frozen to bars, cafés, hotels and pastry kitchens across Sri Lanka.

faqs.q: Is fruit puree the same as a flavoured syrup?
faqs.a: No. Puree is the fruit itself, pulped and strained. A flavoured syrup is mostly sugar with flavouring and colour. Puree gives real fruit taste and body.

faqs.q: How should frozen fruit puree be thawed?
faqs.a: Thaw it overnight in the refrigerator, keep it chilled once thawed, and use it within the time stated on the pack. Don't refreeze thawed puree.

title: Imported cheese for Sri Lankan kitchens: types, uses and storage
seoTitle: Imported Cheese in Sri Lanka: Types, Uses and Storage
description: Which imported cheeses hotel, restaurant and café kitchens in Sri Lanka use, for melting, grating, crumbling and cheese boards, and how to store them so they keep.
summary: Most hotel and restaurant menus in Sri Lanka are covered by four kinds of cheese: a melting cheese (Gouda, Cheddar, Emmental or processed slices), a grating cheese (Grana Padano, Parmesan or Pecorino Romano), a crumbling cheese (feta, young goat cheese or Danish blue) and a cheese for boards (aged Gouda or Comté). Olive Foods imports and distributes all of these, most from Daily Dairy in the Netherlands, and supplies hotels, restaurants, cafés and retailers island-wide.

sections.heading: Melting cheeses: burgers, sandwiches, pizza and bakes
paragraphs: Gouda is a semi-hard Dutch cheese that melts smoothly, which makes it a good all-rounder for toasties, burgers, pasta bakes and pizza. Edam is milder and firmer, good for slicing and snacking. Cheddar, white or coloured (usually with annatto, a natural colouring), brings a sharper flavour to burgers, wraps and macaroni cheese. Emmental, the Swiss-style cheese with holes, melts into sauces, gratins and fondue. Processed cheese slices melt fastest and most evenly, which is why quick-service burger lines use them.

sections.heading: Grating cheeses: pasta, risotto and salads
paragraphs: Grana Padano is a protected Italian cheese made from cow's milk and aged for at least nine months. It is the everyday grating cheese of Italian kitchens. Pecorino Romano is made from sheep's milk and is saltier and sharper: it is the traditional cheese for carbonara and cacio e pepe. Ready-grated Parmesan saves time on busy lines; for the best flavour, grate wedges to order.

sections.heading: Crumbling cheeses: salads, pastries and toppings
paragraphs: Feta is a brined Greek cheese for salads, pastries and baked dishes; keep it in its brine so it stays moist. Young goat cheese is mild and creamy, for salads, tarts and spreading on bread. Danish blue is sharp and creamy, for dressings, steak and burger toppings and cheese boards.

sections.heading: Cheeses for boards
paragraphs: For a cheese board, pair a hard cheese with a soft one and a blue. Comté is a hard French cow's-milk cheese with a nutty flavour. V.S.O.C Black Label is an extra-aged Gouda with crunchy crystals that form during long ageing. Serve board cheeses at room temperature: take them out of the refrigerator 30 to 60 minutes before service.

sections.heading: Reading the label: what 48% means
paragraphs: The percentage on Dutch-style cheeses, such as Gouda 48% or Edam 40%, is the fat content of the cheese's dry matter, not of the whole cheese. Because cheese also contains water, the share of fat in the cheese as you eat it is lower than the number on the label.

sections.heading: Storing cheese
items: Keep cheese refrigerated, between 2 °C and 7 °C.
Wrap cut faces tightly so they don't dry out, and rewrap after each use.
Store blue cheese wrapped and apart from other cheeses.
Keep feta covered in its brine.
Freezing changes the texture of most cheeses, making them crumbly; keep it for cheese that will be cooked or grated.

faqs.q: Where can hotels buy imported cheese in Sri Lanka?
faqs.a: Olive Foods imports and distributes European cheeses (Gouda, Edam, Cheddar, Emmental, Comté, Grana Padano, Pecorino Romano, feta, goat cheese and Danish blue) and supplies hotels, restaurants, cafés and retailers across Sri Lanka.

faqs.q: What is the difference between Grana Padano and Parmigiano Reggiano?
faqs.a: Both are hard Italian grating cheeses made from cow's milk. Parmigiano Reggiano comes from a smaller area under stricter rules and is aged for at least 12 months; Grana Padano is aged for at least nine months and is milder and less expensive.

faqs.q: Which cheese is best for burgers?
faqs.a: Processed cheese slices melt fastest and most evenly, which suits quick-service lines. For more flavour, use Cheddar or Gouda; for a premium burger, a little Danish blue.

title: Italian pasta for restaurants: shapes, sauces and cooking
seoTitle: Italian Pasta for Restaurants in Sri Lanka: Shapes and Cooking
description: A practical guide for restaurant and hotel kitchens in Sri Lanka: which pasta shape goes with which sauce, how to cook dried pasta for service, and how much to allow per portion.
summary: Dried durum-wheat pasta is the backbone of an Italian menu: it keeps for months, cooks in minutes and holds its bite. Choose the shape for the sauce (long strands for oil and light tomato sauces, ribbons for cream and ragù, tubes and twists for chunky sauces and bakes), allow 80–100 g of dried pasta for a main course, and cook it in plenty of well-salted water. Olive Foods imports Dedicato pasta from Granoro in Puglia and Donna Chiara pasta, plus semolina lasagna sheets, for restaurants and hotels across Sri Lanka.

sections.heading: Match the shape to the sauce

head: Shape

sections.heading: Cooking dried pasta for service
paragraphs: Italian cooks follow a simple rule: 1 litre of water and about 10 g of salt for every 100 g of pasta. Plenty of water keeps the temperature up when the pasta goes in and stops it sticking. Start tasting a minute or two before the time on the pack and drain when the pasta is al dente, tender with a slight bite in the centre.

Busy kitchens par-cook: boil the pasta for about two minutes less than the pack time, drain, spread it out or toss it with a little oil to cool, and portion it. At service, drop a portion into boiling water for a minute, or finish it directly in the hot sauce. Keep a little of the cooking water: its starch helps sauces cling to the pasta.

sections.heading: Portions and yield
paragraphs: Allow 80–100 g of dried pasta for a main course and 50–60 g for a starter or side. Dried pasta roughly doubles to two-and-a-half times its weight when cooked, so a 1 kg pack gives about 10 to 12 main-course portions.

sections.heading: Why durum wheat
paragraphs: Italian dried pasta is made from durum wheat semolina, a hard, high-protein wheat whose gluten keeps pasta firm when cooked; Italian law requires it for dried pasta made in Italy. Dedicato is Granoro's 100% Puglia line, built on durum wheat grown in Puglia through a supply chain linking local farms, mills and Granoro's pasta factory in Corato.

sections.heading: Storing
paragraphs: Keep dried pasta sealed in a cool, dry place, off the floor and away from strong smells. Stored this way it keeps until the best-before date on the pack.

faqs.q: How much dried pasta should I allow per person?
faqs.a: Allow 80–100 g of dried pasta for a main course and 50–60 g for a starter or side. Dried pasta roughly doubles to two-and-a-half times its weight when cooked.

faqs.q: Which pasta shapes are best for baked dishes?
faqs.a: Tubes and twists such as penne, fusilli and elbow macaroni hold sauce and cheese in a bake; lasagna sheets and cannelloni are made for layered and filled baked dishes.

faqs.a: Olive Foods imports Dedicato and Donna Chiara pasta and semolina lasagna sheets and supplies restaurants, hotels, cafés and retailers across Sri Lanka. Send a quote request with the shapes and quantities you need.

title: Frozen fries and potato products for hotels and quick-service kitchens
seoTitle: Frozen French Fries in Sri Lanka: A Guide for Kitchens
description: How restaurant, hotel and quick-service kitchens in Sri Lanka choose and cook frozen fries, wedges and hash browns: cut sizes, coated fries, frying temperature and oil care.
summary: Frozen fries are potatoes that have been cut, blanched, usually par-fried and frozen, so a kitchen only has to finish them: most are fried straight from frozen at around 175 °C, or as the pack directs, until golden. The cut decides the result. Thin cuts are crisper and faster, thicker cuts fluffier inside, and coated fries hold their crunch longer for delivery and buffets. Olive Foods imports Hungritos 9 mm fries, coated 7 mm shoestring fries, potato wedges and hash browns, and delivers them at −18 °C.

head: Product
Character
Use it for
rows: Everyday sides, kids' menus, room service
Thin, extra crunchy, made to stay crisp longer

sections.heading: Frying for the best result
items: Fry straight from frozen. Thawed fries soak up oil and turn limp.
Heat the oil to around 175 °C, or as the pack says, before the fries go in.
Fill the basket no more than halfway: too many frozen fries at once drop the oil temperature and the fries steam instead of crisping.
Shake the basket once or twice, drain well and salt away from the fryer; salt falling into the oil breaks it down faster.
Serve straight away, or choose coated fries where they have to wait.

sections.heading: Looking after the oil
paragraphs: Fry oil decides the taste of the fries. Skim crumbs during service, filter the oil daily, top it up with fresh oil, and change it when it turns dark, smokes at normal frying temperature, foams, or starts to smell. Fry fish and battered foods in a separate fryer if you can, so the fries don't pick up the flavour.

sections.heading: Wedges and hash browns
paragraphs: Both cook from frozen, in the fryer or in a hot oven. Oven-baking suits breakfast buffets and large batches: spread them in a single layer and turn them halfway through.

sections.heading: Storage
paragraphs: Keep frozen potato products at −18 °C and close opened bags tightly. Fries that thaw and refreeze stick together in clumps and lose their texture, so move deliveries into the freezer straight away.

faqs.q: What temperature should frozen fries be cooked at?
faqs.a: Fry frozen fries at around 175 °C, or the temperature given on the pack, until golden. Don't overfill the basket, or the oil temperature drops and the fries go soggy.

faqs.q: Should frozen fries be thawed before frying?
faqs.a: Usually not. Most frozen fries are made to be cooked straight from frozen, so follow the pack. Thawed fries absorb more oil and come out limp.

faqs.a: Olive Foods imports Hungritos frozen fries (9 mm and coated 7 mm shoestring), potato wedges and hash browns, and delivers them at −18 °C to restaurants, hotels and caterers across Sri Lanka.

title: Mexican ingredients in Sri Lanka: tortillas and hot sauce
seoTitle: Mexican Ingredients in Sri Lanka: Tortillas, Hot Sauce and More
description: How restaurants and cafés in Sri Lanka build a Mexican menu: choosing tortilla sizes, warming and storing tortillas, and the imported and local ingredients for burritos, tacos and quesadillas.
summary: A Mexican menu in Sri Lanka starts with flour tortillas: 10-inch for burritos, wraps and quesadillas, 6-inch for tacos and fajitas. Add beans, sweet corn and melting cheese, a hot sauce such as Tabasco, and local tomatoes, onions, coriander, chillies, limes and avocados, and you can cover most of the dishes guests expect. Olive Foods imports Albertos tortillas, Tabasco, red kidney beans, sweet corn and Cheddar and supplies them to restaurants, cafés and hotels island-wide.

sections.heading: Choosing a tortilla size
items: 10-inch wraps (6 per pack): burritos, wraps, large quesadillas and breakfast burritos.
6-inch wraps (8 per pack): street-style tacos, fajitas, kids' portions and canapés.

sections.heading: Warming and storing tortillas
paragraphs: Tortillas fold without cracking only when warm. Heat each one on a dry pan or griddle for a few seconds a side until soft and lightly spotted, or steam a stack wrapped in a damp cloth. Keep warmed tortillas wrapped in a cloth or tortilla warmer during service.
Reseal opened packs tightly so the tortillas don't dry out, and follow the storage instructions on the pack.

sections.heading: Building the menu
paragraphs: Red kidney beans make chilli and a quick refried-style filling; sweet corn goes into salsas and salads. For quesadillas and burritos, use a cheese that melts well, such as Cheddar or Gouda. Fresh salsa (pico de gallo) and guacamole are made with local tomatoes, onions, coriander, chillies, limes and avocados.

sections.heading: Tabasco in the kitchen and at the bar
paragraphs: Tabasco Original Red is made from tabasco peppers, vinegar and salt, so it adds acidity as well as heat. A few drops lift salsas, marinades, eggs, pizza and seafood, and it is the classic seasoning in a Bloody Mary. Put bottles on tables for guests who like more heat.

faqs.q: Where can I buy tortillas wholesale in Sri Lanka?
faqs.a: Olive Foods imports Albertos flour tortillas in 10-inch (6 per pack) and 6-inch (8 per pack) sizes and supplies restaurants, cafés, hotels and caterers across Sri Lanka.

faqs.q: What size tortilla is used for burritos?
faqs.a: Burritos need a large tortilla, 10 inches or more, so the filling can be wrapped and the ends folded in. Six-inch tortillas are the usual size for tacos.

faqs.q: How do you stop tortillas cracking?
faqs.a: Warm them before filling, on a dry pan or griddle for a few seconds a side or steamed in a damp cloth, and keep them wrapped until use.
